extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of dramatic theory composing tragic drama
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing tragedy: how to design plot, parts, character, and incidents so as to produce pity and fear (per Aristotle's Poetics). Emphasises unity, causal sequence, peripeteia/anagnorisis, and appropriate characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper magnitude (length) of the plot
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper magnitude is comprised within such limits that the sequence of events, according to the law of probability or necessity, will admit of a change from bad fortune to good, or from good fortune to bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length should be such that the whole can be easily embraced by memory; greater length can be more beautiful by reason of size provided the whole be perspicuous. The limit fixed by competition (e.g. a water-clock) is not artistic theory — the intrinsic nature of the drama sets the proper length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (unity of plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot must imitate one action and that a whole, the structural union of the parts being such that, if any one of them is displaced or removed, the whole will be disjointed and disturbed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity of the hero is not unity of plot — many incidents in one life cannot be reduced to one action. An organic whole: nothing whose presence or absence makes no visible difference is a part. Examples: Homer omitted many episodes to keep unity in the Iliad and Odyssey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal sequence: probability or necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot's sequence of events must follow according to the law of probability or necessity rather than arbitrary or disconnected episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events should follow as cause and effect so that changes (peripeteia, etc.) appear necessary or probable. This causal logic is essential to produce the tragic effects and to avoid episodic incoherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry represents the possible/universal (not merely history)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not the function of the poet to relate what has happened, but what may happen—what is possible according to the law of probability or necessity. Poetry tends to express the universal; history the particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet's subject may be historical yet poetic if the events conform to the probable/possible. Emphasise types and universals (how a person of a certain type will act) more than mere particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid episodic (epeisodic) plots
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'epeisodic' plot is one in which the episodes or acts succeed one another without probable or necessary sequence; of all plots these are the worst.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad poets produce episodic plots by fault; good poets sometimes are forced by actors/competition to stretch plots, producing broken continuity. Do not compose sequences that lack causal or probable connexion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy must imitate actions inspiring pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of a complete action and of events inspiring fear or pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tragic effect is best when events come by surprise and follow as cause and effect. The inner structure (not spectacle) should produce pity and fear. Coincidences are most striking when they seem designed rather than accidental (e.g., the statue of Mitys).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer complex plots (peripeteia and/or anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are Simple or Complex. A Complex action is one in which the change of fortune is accompanied by Reversal (peripeteia), or by Recognition (anagnorisis), or by both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots, where reversal/recognition arise from the plot's internal structure, are superior for tragedy because they heighten pity and fear. The reversal/recognition should be organic, not contrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Simple plot
rubrics_metrics.description: A Simple action is one and continuous in the defined sense: the change of fortune takes place without Reversal of the Situation and without Recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple plots lack peripeteia/anagnorisis; they are continuous but less powerful for tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of the Situation (peripeteia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal is a change by which the action veers round to its opposite, subject always to the rule of probability or necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversal should arise naturally from preceding incidents (e.g., the messenger in Oedipus who intends to comfort but instead brings doom). It must be credible within the plot's causal economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge, producing love or hate between persons destined for good or bad fortune; best when coincident with Reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most powerful recognition is of persons and when combined with reversal produces the strongest pity and fear. Recognitions may also involve inanimate signs or discoveries of acts performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene of suffering (pathos) as an essential part
rubrics_metrics.description: The Scene of Suffering is a destructive or painful action, such as death on the stage, bodily agony, wounds and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peripeteia and recognition are two parts of the plot; the scene of suffering (pathos) is the third. These elements together generate the tragic effect when properly integrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative parts of tragedy (prologue, episode, exode, choric song)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy's parts: Prologue, Episode, Exode, Choric song—and of the choric song the Parode and the Stasimon; also the Commos and other scene-songs peculiar to some plays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions: Prologue = part preceding chorus' parode; Episode = parts between choric songs; Exode = final part without choric song after it. Parode = first utterance of Chorus; Stasimon = choric ode without marching meters; Commos = lament between Chorus and actors. These quantitative divisions should be observed in construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot should show change from good to bad by error (hamartia)
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of fortune should come about as the result not of vice, but of some great error or frailty in a character who is highly renowned and prosperous (neither eminently good-and-just nor utterly villainous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make the hero a paragon who falls (moves neither pity nor fear) nor an utter villain whose downfall only satisfies moral sense without producing pity. Prefer characters like Oedipus, Thyestes: renowned men whose fall arises from error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-issue (unity of outcome) preferred to double plot
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-constructed plot should be single in its issue rather than double as some maintain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-thread plots (like the Odyssey) are lower in rank, often catering to spectator weakness; single outcome plots produce truer tragic effect when well executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of plot over verse (poet as maker of plots)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should be the maker of plots rather than of verses; since he is a poet because he imitates actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The maker imitates actions; even if a historical subject is used, the poet's art is judged by how well the plot conforms to probable/possible actions, not merely by metrical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer inner-structure effects to spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity may be aroused by spectacle, but they may also result from the inner structure of the piece—which is the better and indicates a superior poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the plot so that hearing the tale (without visual aids) produces horror and pity. Avoid relying on monstrous spectacle which creates only the sense of the monstrous, not true tragic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use or adaptation of traditional myths with invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet need not rigidly adhere to received legends; he ought to show invention of his own and skilfully handle traditional material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though some facts (e.g., Clytemnestra slain by Orestes) may be retained, the poet should adapt and manage the received stories well. Known subjects may be obscure to most spectators yet still pleasurable; fictitious names and invented incidents may be used effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic relationship of agents (friends, enemies, kinship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions that produce pity or terror should occur among those who are friends, enemies, or indifferent; particularly effective are deeds between those near or dear (e.g., brother killing brother, son killing father).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kinship or close relationships heighten pity/fear; plan incidents so ties of family or friendship are central to the tragic action. Examples: Orestes/Clytemnestra, Alcmaeon/Eriphyle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and manner of the dreadful deed (rank of modes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dreadful deed may be (a) done knowingly, (b) done in ignorance and recognized afterwards, (c) one is about to act knowing the persons and then does not act (worst), (d) about to act in ignorance and recognises before acting. The best is when the deed is perpetrated in ignorance and discovered afterwards (produces startling effect); the worst is preparing knowingly and then not acting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer modes that avoid mere shock without tragedy. The most effective tragic arrangements produce recognition and reversal in ways that heighten pity/fear (e.g., Oedipus, Merope). Avoid scenarios that are shocking but not tragic (no disaster follows).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the episodic stretching of plot for theatrical display
rubrics_metrics.description: Playwrights sometimes stretch the plot beyond its capacity to please players or meet competitive demands, producing episodic or concatenated incidents without natural continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not insert disconnected spectacles or superfluous episodes merely to display actors or to lengthen performance; such practices break unity and weaken tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character suitability and consistency (ethos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters' moral qualities and dispositions must be appropriate and consistent—'how they should be' (e.g., a character may be good or base in degree, but traits must fit the person's sex, station, and role).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider: first, whether the character is 'good' or at least not utterly base; second, what traits are fitting (e.g., courage may not be fitting for a woman in traditional representation); third, likeness—characters should be similar to what is expected for their sort. Ethos must manifest in speech and action so that the audience perceives premeditation or choice where appropriate.
